content.overview: BNS s. 106 — Causing death by negligence.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide (old 304A). Clause (1) is in force: up to 5 years (8 if a registered medical practitioner in the course of a medical procedure). Clause (2) — causing death by rash driving and fleeing — was not commenced.
In student language: BNS s. 106 is the rule on “Causing death by negligence”. The section provides that (1) Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 106 exists so that “Causing death by negligence” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
106. (1) Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine

Definitions and key terms
“registered medical practitioner” — a medical practitioner who possesses any medical qualification recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 and whose name has been entered in the National Medical Register or a State Medical Register under that Act (2) Whoever causes death of any person by rash and negligent driving of vehicle not amounting to culpable homicide, and escapes without reporting it to a police officer or a Magistrate soon after the incident, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description of a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Essential ingredients
1. (1) Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine

Punishment / legal consequence
(1) up to 5 years (8 if medical). (2) hit-and-run up to 10 years — not in force.

Explanations
Explanation.— For the purposes of this sub-section, “registered medical practitioner” means a medical practitioner who possesses any medical qualification recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 and whose name has been entered in the National Medical Register or a State Medical Register under that Act

(2) Whoever causes death of any person by rash and negligent driving of vehicle not amounting to culpable homicide, and escapes without reporting it to a police officer or a Magistrate soon after the incident, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description of a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. (Section 106(2) of BNS shall not come into force on 1 st July 2024)

sections.heading: Commencement status
sections.body: Section 106(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 has not been brought into force by the commencement notification located for this review. Ministry of Home Affairs Notification S.O. 850(E), dated 23 February 2024, appoints 1 July 2024 as the commencement date for the Sanhita except section 106(2). The Ministry of Home Affairs also records this exception in its parliamentary answer dated 30 July 2024. Treat section 106(2) as enacted text with commencement excluded on the evidence checked; do not describe its punishment as operative law unless a later official commencement notification is located. Re-check the Gazette before final legal sign-off.

enhancement.definition: BNS s. 106 governs causing death by negligence. Under sub-section (1), whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment up to two years and fine. Under sub-section (2), whoever causes the death of any person by rash and negligent driving of vehicle not amounting to culpable homicide, and escapes without reporting it to a police officer or a Magistrate soon after the incident, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Public safety on roadways, deterrence against vehicular abandonment of victims, and professional criminal negligence standards. Section 106 balances the duty of drivers to render aid and report accidents with protected standards of gross negligence for registered medical professionals.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 106.
Sub-section (1): General rash or negligent act causing death (punishable up to 5 years, increased from 2 years under old s. 304A IPC).
Sub-section (1) Proviso: Medical negligence by registered medical practitioners performing medical procedures (punishment capped at 2 years).

Sub-section (2): Aggravated Hit-and-Run offence — rash/negligent driving causing death accompanied by escaping without reporting to police or Magistrate soon after (punishable up to 10 years and fine).
essentialIngredients: The death of a human being caused by the act of the accused.
The act was rash (reckless hazard with indifference to consequences) or negligent (omission of duty of care expected of a reasonable person).
The act does not amount to culpable homicide (absence of intention or knowledge of imminent death).
For the aggravated offence under Sub-section (2):
(a) The death was caused by rash and negligent driving of a vehicle; and
(b) The driver escaped without reporting the accident to a police officer or a Magistrate soon after the incident.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 106 BNS modernizes the law governing unintentional homicide, addressing the epidemic of road traffic fatalities in India. It fundamentally reforms Section 304A of the repealed IPC by creating a tiered sentencing structure.

Under the old law (s. 304A IPC), the maximum sentence for causing death by negligence was merely two years imprisonment, regardless of whether the driver stayed to assist or fled leaving the victim to bleed to death on the highway. Section 106 introduces a decisive bifurcation:

1. **General Negligence (s. 106(1)):** Increases the general punishment for causing death by rash or negligent act from two years to five years imprisonment.
2. **Medical Negligence Proviso (s. 106(1)):** Recognizes the unique professional risks faced by doctors. Under the statutory proviso, if death is caused by a registered medical practitioner while performing a medical procedure, the punishment is restricted to imprisonment up to two years and fine. This incorporates the established *Jacob Mathew* doctrine: criminal liability attaches only where negligence is gross, reckless, or flagrant, not for a mere error of clinical judgment.
3. **Aggravated Hit-and-Run (s. 106(2)):** Enacts a stringent penalty of up to ten years imprisonment and fine for drivers who cause fatal accidents by rash and negligent driving and escape without reporting the incident to the police or a Magistrate soon after. The objective is to encourage drivers to stop, provide medical assistance (or summon an ambulance), and report immediately, saving lives during the critical "golden hour".
examples: Teaching illustration (Section 106(2) Hit-and-Run): A commercial truck driver drives at 90 km/h in a crowded urban market, hits a pedestrian on a zebra crossing causing fatal injuries, and accelerates away without stopping or reporting to the nearest police station or Magistrate. The driver is arrested three days later. The driver is liable under Section 106(2) BNS and subject to imprisonment extending up to ten years.

Teaching illustration (Section 106(1) Compliance / Non-Hit-and-Run): A car driver accidentally strikes a bicyclist who suddenly veered into the lane. The driver immediately stops, calls emergency medical services, takes the injured cyclist to a hospital where the cyclist unfortunately succumbs to injuries, and reports the event to the police officer at the hospital. Because the driver did not escape and reported the incident, Section 106(2) does not apply; liability is evaluated solely under Section 106(1).
distinctions: BNS s. 106(1) vs BNS s. 106(2): Sub-section (1) applies to general negligence (up to 5 years); Sub-section (2) applies exclusively to vehicular driving where the driver escapes without reporting the accident soon after (up to 10 years).

Rashness vs Negligence: Rashness is acting with consciousness that consequences may result, but with reckless hope that they will not; Negligence is a breach of duty caused by inadvertence or omission to do something which a reasonable person would do.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a surgeon whose patient dies during a complex heart surgery can be prosecuted under Section 106(1) BNS for general criminal negligence carrying 5 years imprisonment.

Rule: Under the proviso to Section 106(1) BNS, where death is caused by a registered medical practitioner performing a medical procedure, the punishment is restricted to a maximum of two years, and criminal liability requires proof of gross, culpable negligence beyond civil error.
Application: The surgeon performed the surgery according to accepted medical standards; complication arose due to rare cardiac arrest. No gross criminal recklessness is demonstrated on record.
Conclusion: The surgeon is not criminally liable under Section 106(1); even if criminal negligence were alleged, the proviso limits punishment to two years.

keyTakeaways: Section 106(1) increases general punishment for causing death by negligence from 2 years to 5 years.
Registered medical practitioners performing procedures are subject to a maximum punishment of 2 years under the proviso.
Section 106(2) creates an aggravated hit-and-run offence punishable with up to 10 years imprisonment for drivers who flee without reporting.
Drivers who stop and report the accident to the police or Magistrate avoid the aggravated penalty of Section 106(2).
